title: The school
hookLine: the madrasah teaching Qur'an, law, language and more

lines: A HALF CIRCLE ON THE FLOOR.
cards: A pillar in a big mosque. A teacher sits with his back against it, a book open on his knees. Around him on the floor, in a half circle, his students: a boy from the town, an old merchant, a traveler who arrived last week.
He reads a line, explains it, and they write. When the lesson ends, they stand up and the circle disappears. Tomorrow it forms again at the same pillar.
That circle is called a halaqa, and learning in Muslim lands often happened in circles like it, before there was any building called a school. Today: the school.

teach.b: A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in Sahih Muslim, makes a promise: whoever travels a road seeking knowledge, God makes easy for them a road to paradise. So people traveled, and sat in circles.

Over time the circles needed rooms, food, books and paid teachers, and the madrasah grew around them. You met the great colleges of Baghdad and Fez earlier on this path. Today, step inside an ordinary one.
A courtyard with a fountain. Small rooms around it where students lived. A prayer hall.
A shelf of books. Classes in Qur'an and hadith, law and Arabic grammar, and in some, logic or arithmetic. And at the end, no diploma from the building.
Instead, a person. You met the calligrapher's license a few days ago; the schools had their own.
A teacher could give you an ijazah, written permission to teach a book, naming who had taught it to him, and who had taught that teacher, back through a chain of names.
The knowledge belonged to the chain, not to the walls.
One more surprise: in Arabic, madrasah simply means school.

teach.h: THE IJAZAH: A CHAIN OF TEACHERS.
teach.b: Any school. A child in Cairo goes to a madrasah to learn math and science.

how: Muslim children and adults study in mosque circles and madrasahs of every kind, from weekend Qur'an classes to seminaries; in traditional study a student may still receive an ijazah from a teacher, naming the chain of teachers behind it.

o: a building that hands out diplomas to its graduates
places to learn, from a mosque circle to a college
a seminary that trains only future prayer leaders

p: a study circle around a teacher
permission to teach, with a chain of names
a road to knowledge, a road to paradise

s: in Arabic, madrasah means only a religious school
it simply means school; a child in Cairo goes to a madrasah to learn math and science.
an ijazah named the chain of teachers behind the one who gave it
the knowledge belonged to the chain, not to the walls.
Muslim learning began inside purpose-built school buildings
it grew in study circles in the mosque, the halaqa, before the madrasah.

games.q: you've studied a book with your teacher for a long time and want to teach it yourself. what do you need?
o: your teacher's ijazah, naming the chain behind him.
games.why: the ijazah came from a person, not a building: written permission to teach that book, with the chain of teachers behind it.

practice: Bring back one place where you learned something that stayed, a classroom, a mosque circle, a library, a kitchen table, and one teacher there. What did they hand you that you still carry?
If you pray, you can pray for them, living or gone; if you don't, just hold their face in mind for a moment.

wordCard.voice: The school. From the halaqa at a mosque pillar to the madrasah with its courtyard, its students and its chain of teachers. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: places to learn. The knowledge lived in people, passed hand to hand. Until tomorrow.
